scenes.tts: Stop mowing a field in the Virginia Piedmont. Nobody plants anything. Seeds blow in or wait in the soil. Within a few years, the field can fill with broomsedge, blackberry and small pines. After a century or more, oaks and hickories can take over. What happens to a field after people or fire leave it alone?

scenes.tts: This change has a name: ecological succession. A community is all the populations of different species living in one area. Succession is the change, over years to centuries, in which species live there. The change often follows a general pattern. Certain plants tend to come early, others late.
scenes.visual: Community box of coloured dots changes mix over three boxes along a time arrow; early dots lime, late dots orange.
scenes.narration: This change has a name: ecological succession. A community is all the populations of different species living in one area. scenes.tts: Succession often starts after a disturbance. A disturbance is an event, like a fire, flood or plowing, that removes much of a community. If the soil stays, it is secondary succession. On bare rock there is no soil. That is primary succession, and lichens and mosses usually arrive first. Secondary succession usually reaches forest much faster.
scenes.visual: A community block is hit by a red disturbance; splits into a soil-stays ground bar (secondary) and a bare-rock bar (primary) with lichen blobs; a faster/slower pair of arrows.

scenes.tts: Here is the usual path published for old Piedmont fields, just south of Virginia. In the first years, weeds such as horseweed and asters grow fast in full sun. By about the third year, broomsedge, a tall grass, often covers the field. Pines grow fast in full sun. Within a few decades, the field becomes a young pine forest.
scenes.visual: Field cross-section in four columns along a timeline: weeds, broomsedge, young pines, with a sun and arrows of light reaching the plants.

scenes.tts: Each stage changes the place it grows in. Abiotic factors are the nonliving parts of an ecosystem, such as light and soil. A closed pine canopy blocks much of the sunlight. Pine seedlings grow poorly in that shade. Young hardwoods cope with shade better. Oaks and hickories can survive some shade, but they grow best where a gap lets in light. As the old pines die, the hardwoods fill the gaps.
scenes.visual: Zoom on the pine stand; sun arrows stop at the canopy; pine seedling shown struggling, hardwood sapling coping; pines fade, hardwoods grow up.

scenes.tts: So why do plants arrive in this order? Each stage changes light and soil, and the plants that cope best with the new conditions take over. In most of Virginia, the late stage has been called an oak-hickory climax community, a hardwood forest. But fire, storms and people reset patches, so the path and timing vary. Each stage changes the place, and the plants that cope best take over.
